mainTopic: Trusting court documents, believing statements about hidden money, writing split verdicts, and joining two witnesses' testimony
overview: The amud opens by finishing a case about a court document signed by only two people. The גמרא worries about a mistaken court that thought two judges were enough, and it concludes that the document can be trusted only when it shows that רב אשי himself took part. A ברייתא then teaches when a statement about hidden money is believed. A witness is believed if he could have taken the money himself. A father is believed if he was truly passing on information rather than using a trick. A dream is not believed at all. The גמרא next asks how a split verdict is written. רבי יוחנן avoids רכילות, ריש לקיש avoids a misleading document, and רבי אלעזר combines both concerns: 'מדבריהם נזדכה פלוני'. Then it asks who is 'brought in' after the judges decide, the witnesses or the litigants. This leads to a ברייתא about joining two witnesses who saw the event at different times, and two witnesses who testified on different days. For each argument the גמרא offers a reason from logic and a reason from a פסוק, and the פסוק-based explanation of רבי נתן's argument continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The document had full court wording but no mention of a third judge
steps.stepSummary: The case continues: the document used all the standard court wording but did not say 'we were three and one is no longer here.'
steps.simpleTranslation: It had all the standard court wording, but it did not say, 'We sat as three, and one is no longer here.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing its description of a court document whose validity is in question. This sets up the discussion that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Only two names were signed, and a court needs three. Courts usually explain this by writing that a third judge sat with them but is not available to sign. This document left that line out, so we do not know whether a full court of three was ever there.

keyTerms.meaning: The standard wording a court uses in its documents
In a session of three judges

phrases.english: and all the standard wording of the court was in it,
but it did not have written in it:
'We were in a session of three,
and one is no longer here.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the case description from the previous daf.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The case: a two-signature court document with full court wording but no statement that a third judge was present.

steps.title: רבינא first thinks ריש לקיש's rule makes the document valid
steps.stepSummary: רבינא thinks this case falls under ריש לקיש's rule, so we can assume everything was done properly.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא thought to say: this is just the rule of ריש לקיש.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא suggests a way to accept the document: ריש לקיש's rule says witnesses do not sign unless things were done properly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If signers only sign a properly done act, the two signers would not have signed unless a proper court of three had sat. So the missing line would not matter. The word 'סבר' tells us this is only a first idea, and it will be rejected.

keyTerms.meaning: He thought to say (a first idea that is about to be rejected)

steps.confusionAlert: Don't take רבינא's view as the final ruling. 'סבר' signals an idea that the גמרא is about to reject.

phrases.english: Ravina thought to say:
this is the rule of Reish Lakish.
phrases.notes: His rule is that witnesses don't sign a document unless everything was done properly.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a first answer to whether the document from step 1 is valid.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: First idea: the document is valid because signers only sign what was done properly.

steps.title: רב נתן בר אמי: we worry about a court that made a mistake
steps.stepSummary: Quoting רבא, רב נתן בר אמי says that in such cases we worry the signers wrongly thought two judges were enough.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נתן בר אמי said to him: this is what we say in the name of רבא. In every case like this, we worry about a mistaken court.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נתן בר אמי rejects רבינא's idea by quoting רבא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ריש לקיש's rule only helps when the signers knew the right way to do things. Here the worry is that the signers honestly thought a court of two was fine. They were not lying; they simply made a mistake about the law, so the document cannot be trusted.

keyTerms.meaning: A mistaken court, one that thinks two judges are enough

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that a presumption that signers acted properly cannot cover a possible mistake about the law itself.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב נָתָן בַּר אַמֵּי:
phrases.english: Rav Natan bar Ami said to him:
this is what we say in the name of Rava:
in every case like this,
we are concerned about a mistaken court.
phrases.notes: He means judges who honestly but wrongly think two of them make a court.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב נָתָן בַּר אַמֵּי הָכִי אָמְרִינַן מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרָבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects רבינא's idea from step 2.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The use of ריש לקיש's rule to make the document valid.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: ריש לקיש's rule does not protect against signers who were honestly wrong about how many judges are needed.

steps.title: רב נחמן בר יצחק: writing 'the court' is enough
steps.stepSummary: If the document says 'בי דינא' (the court), it does not also need to say that a third judge was there.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן בר יצחק said: if 'the court' is written in it, nothing more is needed.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן בר יצחק gives a way for such a document to be valid: if it calls the signers 'the court.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: A normal court has three judges. So writing 'we, the court' already tells us there were three, even though only two signed. Then the line about the missing judge is not needed.

phrases.english: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says:
if 'the court' is written in it,
nothing more is needed.
phrases.notes: He means it doesn't also need the line 'one of us is no longer here.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק אִי כְּתִב בַּהּ בֵּי דִינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the worry about a mistaken court, gives wording that removes that worry.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A document that says 'the court' is valid even without stating that a third judge was there.

steps.title: Challenge: maybe it was a 'בית דין חצוף' of only two judges
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: even with the word 'court,' maybe it was two judges acting as a court, which שמואל calls a בית דין חצוף.
steps.simpleTranslation: But maybe it was a בית דין חצוף? As שמואל said: two who judged, their ruling is a ruling, but they are called a בית דין חצוף.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב נחמן בר יצחק: the word 'court' does not prove there were three judges.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל says two judges who rule together do make a binding ruling, but they are called a 'בית דין חצוף' because they went against the rabbis' rule of three. Such a pair could still call itself 'the court.' So the word 'court' alone does not prove three judges sat.

keyTerms.meaning: A 'brazen court': two judges who rule without the third the rabbis require
Their ruling counts as a ruling

steps.confusionAlert: A בית דין חצוף's ruling is still binding. They are only criticized for acting without the required three judges.

phrases.english: But maybe it was a brazen court?
As Shmuel said:
two who judged, their ruling is a ruling,
but they are called a brazen court.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב נחמן בר יצחק's ruling from step 4.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that writing 'בי דינא' proves three judges sat.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Two judges can also act as a court (a בית דין חצוף), so 'the court' does not prove there were three.

steps.title: Answer: the document named the court of רבנא אשי
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק's case was a document that said 'the court of רבנא אשי,' a court known to follow the rules.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was one in which was written: 'the court of רבנא אשי.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by narrowing רב נחמן בר יצחק's case to a document naming a known, proper court.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Not every document saying 'court' is enough, only one that names a well-known court. רב אשי's court would not have ruled with only two judges, so there is no worry about a בית דין חצוף.

keyTerms.meaning: רב אשי, here called by the respectful title רבנא

steps.whatToRemember: A two-signature court document is not valid on its own, because we worry about a mistaken court. Naming רב אשי's court is offered as the fix, but step 7 challenges it, and step 8 shows the real proof is that רב אשי himself took part.

phrases.english: It was one in which was written:
'the court of Rabbana Ashi.'

steps.triggerLanguage: דִּכְתִב בַּיהּ בֵּי דִינָא דְּרַבְנָא אָשֵׁי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from step 5.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case (אוקימתא): the ruling applies only when a known court is named.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The word 'court' might come from two judges acting as a בית דין חצוף.
steps.terutzMaskana: When the document names רב אשי's court, we can trust that three judges sat, as the rules require.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Naming a known, proper court makes the document valid even with only two signatures.

steps.title: Maybe רב אשי's sages also followed שמואל
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the previous answer: maybe the sages in רב אשי's court agree with שמואל that two judges are enough.
steps.simpleTranslation: But maybe the sages of רב אשי's court hold like שמואל?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the answer from step 6. Even a famous court might hold that two judges are enough.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 6 said that רב אשי's court is known to follow the rules. The גמרא now asks: what if the sages there agree with שמואל that two judges make a valid court? If so, the document could still come from a court of only two.

keyTerms.meaning: But perhaps (opens a doubt or challenge)
The sages of רב אשי's study hall or court
They hold, they are of the opinion

phrases.english: But perhaps the sages of the court of רב אשי
hold like שמואל?
phrases.notes: This is שמואל from step 5, who says two judges can rule, even though that court is called 'חצוף'.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְדִילְמָא רַבָּנַן דְּבֵי רַב אָשֵׁי כִּשְׁמוּאֵל סְבִירָא לְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer in step 6
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in step 6 that a document from רב אשי's court must have had three judges
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Being a well-known court does not help if its members agree with שמואל that two judges are enough.

steps.title: רב אשי himself was part of the discussion
steps.stepSummary: The document showed that רבנא אשי personally took part, and he would not sit on a two-judge court.
steps.simpleTranslation: The document said: 'And we said to רבנא אשי, and רבנא אשי said to us.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. The wording of the document shows that רב אשי himself was involved.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worry was about the other sages in the court. But this document records a conversation with רב אשי himself. רב אשי would not take part in a two-judge court, so the court must have been proper.

keyTerms.meaning: In which it is written (the document says)
An honorific title, 'our master', used here for רב אשי

steps.whatToRemember: A document from רב אשי's court can be trusted because it shows that רב אשי himself was part of the proceedings.

phrases.english: It was a document in which it was written:
"And we said to רבנא אשי,"
"and רבנא אשי said to us."

steps.triggerLanguage: דִּכְתִיב בַּהּ וַאֲמַרְנָא לֵיהּ לְרַבַּנָא אָשֵׁי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 7
steps.terutzResolutionType: Points to specific wording in the document
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Maybe the sages of רב אשי's court ruled with only two judges, following שמואל.
steps.terutzMaskana: רב אשי personally took part, and he follows the rules, so the court was valid.

steps.title: A witness says the father's hidden money belongs to someone else
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that a single witness's statement about hidden money is believed only when the money was in the field, not when it was in the house.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא teaches: Someone told the heirs, 'I saw your father hide money in a chest, box, or cabinet, and he said it belongs to so-and-so, or that it is מעשר שני.' If it was in the house, his words count for nothing. If it was in the field, his words stand.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic with a ברייתא about when a statement is believed. A single witness says the father's hidden money is not really the father's.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally one witness is not believed. But if the money was hidden in a field, the witness could have quietly taken it for himself. Since he did not, we believe him. In the house he had no such chance, so his word alone does not count.

keyTerms.meaning: Chest, box, and cabinet (types of storage containers)
Second tithe, holy money that must be used in ירושלים

phrases.english: The sages taught:
One person said to them:
phrases.notes: 'Them' means the father's children, the heirs.

phrases.english: I saw your father
hide money in a chest, box, or cabinet,
and he said, "They belong to so-and-so,"
or, "They are second tithe" —
if it was in the house, he has said nothing;
if it was in the field, his words stand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a new topic about when a statement is believed
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A single witness about hidden money is believed if the money was in the field, but not if it was in the house.

steps.title: The general rule: could he have taken it?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא states the principle behind the house and field cases: he is believed whenever he could have taken the money.
steps.simpleTranslation: The principle is this: whenever it is in his power to take the money, his words stand. If it is not in his power to take it, his words count for nothing.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא explains the reason behind the house and field cases by giving one general rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The real test is not the location itself but whether the witness could have taken the money. If he could have kept it and instead gave it away, he has no reason to lie. If he could not reach it, nothing backs up his word.

keyTerms.meaning: The principle of the matter, the general rule
It is in his power to take them
He has said nothing (his words have no effect)

steps.confusionAlert: The house and field are only examples. What matters is whether the witness could have taken the money, not where it was.

phrases.english: The principle of the matter is:
Whenever it is in his power to take them —
his words stand;
if it is not in his power to take them —
he has said nothing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the general principle behind the cases in step 9
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A witness is believed about money he could have taken for himself, and not about money he could not have taken.

steps.title: When the father himself tells his children
steps.stepSummary: If the children saw their father hide money and he said it belongs to someone else, it depends on whether he was truly informing them or using a trick.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the children saw their father hide money in a chest, box, or cabinet, and he said, 'It belongs to so-and-so' or 'It is מעשר שני': if he said it like someone passing on information, his words stand. If he said it like someone using a trick, his words count for nothing.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives a second case. Here the father himself tells his children that the hidden money is not his.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the question is not whether a witness could have taken the money. The question is what the father really meant. If he was truly telling them a fact, we believe him. If he only said it to scare them away from spending the money, it means nothing and the money is theirs.

keyTerms.meaning: Like one who passes on information (speaking truthfully)
Like one who uses a trick or ruse

steps.whatToRemember: A stranger's statement is believed only if he could have taken the money. A father's statement is believed only if he was truly passing on information, not using a trick.

phrases.english: If they saw their father
hide money in a chest, box, or cabinet,
and he said, "They belong to so-and-so,"
or, "They are second tithe" —
if he said it like one passing on information, his words stand;
if he said it like one using a trick, he has said nothing.
phrases.notes: A trick here means he said it only so the children wouldn't touch the money, not because it was true.

steps.triggerLanguage: הֲרֵי שֶׁרָאוּ אֶת אֲבִיהֶן שֶׁהִטְמִין מָעוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא with a second case, where the father speaks instead of an outside witness
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A father's statement about hidden money is believed if he was truly informing his children, but not if he was using a trick.

steps.title: A dream says the inherited money is second tithe
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא tells of a man whose dream told him how much money his father left, where it was, and that it was מעשר שני. The חכמים ruled that dreams have no effect on הלכה.
steps.simpleTranslation: A man was upset because he could not find the money his father left him. Someone came to him in a dream and said: it is this much, it is in this place, and it is מעשר שני. This really happened, and the חכמים said: what appears in dreams neither adds nor takes away.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא about hidden money continues with one more case, this time about a dream. The חכמים rule that the dream's claim that the money is מעשר שני does not count.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The dream got the amount and the place right, so we might think we should also trust its claim that the money is מעשר שני. The חכמים say no. A dream is not a source for הלכה, so the money keeps its ordinary status and he may use it.

keyTerms.meaning: Literally 'the master of the dream': the figure who speaks to a person in his dream
Second tithe: money with special holiness that may only be spent on food eaten in ירושלים
Literally 'do not raise and do not lower': they make no difference to the halacha

steps.whatToRemember: Even when a dream turns out to be correct about some facts, it has no power to set הלכה. Dreams neither add nor take away.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the dream is ignored because it was wrong. It was right about the amount and the place. It still cannot decide the money's halachic status.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets a broad principle: information from dreams is not a valid source for הלכה.

phrases.english: In a case where one was distressed about money
that his father left him,
and the master of the dream came and said to him:
"It is such and such an amount,"
"it is in such and such a place,"
"it is second tithe."
This was an actual incident, and they said:
matters in dreams
neither raise nor lower.
phrases.notes: In plain words, dreams make no difference to the הלכה.

steps.triggerLanguage: הֲרֵי שֶׁהָיָה מִצְטַעֵר עַל מָעוֹת שֶׁהִנִּיחַ לוֹ אָבִיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a final case to the ברייתא's list of rulings about a father's hidden money.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Dreams have no halachic effect, so money a dream calls מעשר שני is not treated as מעשר שני.

steps.title: How is a split verdict written?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's case where two judges say זכאי and one says חייב, and asks how the verdict is written.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: if two judges say he is exempt (and one says liable, he is exempt). How do they write the verdict?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the משנה and asks a practical question about the written verdict. This sets up the answers in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה tells us the outcome of a split decision, but not how it appears in writing. The question is whether the written verdict should show that the judges disagreed.

keyTerms.meaning: When writing, how do they write?

phrases.english: Two say he is exempt, etc.
phrases.notes: This quotes the משנה. The case is two judges saying exempt and one saying liable.

phrases.english: When writing, how do they write it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the topic of hidden money and returns to the משנה's case of judges who disagree.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The exact wording of a verdict when the judges were not unanimous.

steps.title: Three ways to word the verdict
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן says the verdict simply says 'exempt.' ריש לקיש says it names which judges ruled each way. רבי אליעזר says it states that he was found exempt 'from their words.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן says: write "exempt." ריש לקיש says: write "So-and-so and so-and-so find him exempt, and so-and-so and so-and-so find him liable." רבי אליעזר says: write "From their words, so-and-so was found exempt."
steps.whatsHappening: Three אמוראים give three different wordings for the written verdict.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן's wording hides the disagreement completely. ריש לקיש's wording shows it fully, naming each judge and how he ruled. רבי אליעזר's wording is in between: it hints that the judges were not all in agreement, but it does not say who ruled which way.

keyTerms.meaning: So-and-so: a stand-in for a name
From their words he was found exempt

phrases.english: Rabbi Yoḥanan says: "Exempt."
Reish Lakish says:
"So-and-so and so-and-so deem him exempt,
and so-and-so and so-and-so deem him liable."
Rabbi Eliezer says:
"From their statements, so-and-so was deemed exempt."
phrases.notes: This hints that not every judge agreed, without naming anyone.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of how the verdict is written.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: There are three wordings: plain 'exempt' (רבי יוחנן), naming each judge's view (ריש לקיש), or 'from their words he was found exempt' (רבי אליעזר).

steps.title: What is the practical difference?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what practical difference there is between these opinions.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the difference between them?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks whether these wordings change anything in practice, beyond the words on the page. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The three opinions could seem like a mere argument about style. The גמרא wants to find a real difference in הלכה that depends on the wording.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the difference between them?

phrases.english: What is the difference between them?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks what practical result follows from the three wordings just given.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The practical difference in הלכה between the three wordings.

steps.title: Does the minority judge pay his share?
steps.stepSummary: The difference is whether the judge in the minority must pay his share along with the others. Under 'זכאי' he pays. Under the wording that names each judge, he does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: The difference between them is whether he must pay his portion along with them. According to the one who says to write "exempt," he pays. According to the one who says to write "so-and-so find him exempt and so-and-so find him liable," he does not pay.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the wording decides whether the minority judge must pay his share. This matters in a case where the judges have to pay because the verdict was wrong.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the verdict just says 'exempt,' the record shows no disagreement, so the minority judge looks like part of the ruling and pays along with the others. If the verdict names who ruled each way, it is clear he disagreed, so he does not pay. This is only a first suggestion; the next step challenges it.

phrases.english: There is a difference between them
regarding whether he pays a portion along with them,
phrases.notes: 'He' is the judge in the minority. This is about a case where the judges must pay because their verdict was wrong.

phrases.english: as according to the one who says "exempt," he pays,
and according to the one who says "so-and-so and so-and-so deem him exempt
and so-and-so and so-and-so deem him liable," he does not pay.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא בֵּינַיְיהוּ לְשַׁלּוֹמֵי אִיהוּ מְנָתָא בַּהֲדַיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of what practical difference the wordings make.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Under רבי יוחנן's wording the minority judge pays his share. Under ריש לקיש's wording he does not pay.

steps.title: Why should the outvoted judge have to pay?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא attacks the previous answer. The judge who voted the other way can tell the others that if they had listened to him, nobody would be paying.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to the one who writes just 'זכאי', does the outvoted judge really pay? He can say to them: 'If you had listened to me, you wouldn't be paying either!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the difference it just suggested in Step 16. That difference said the minority judge pays his share under the 'זכאי' wording.
steps.deeperAnalysis: It makes no sense to make the minority judge pay for a mistake he argued against. Even if the written verdict hides his vote, he can still claim he was right all along. So the wording of the verdict should not make him pay.

keyTerms.meaning: According to the one who says

phrases.english: And according to the one who says 'exempt,' he pays?!
phrases.notes: 'He' is the one judge who voted חייב and was outvoted.

phrases.english: Let him say to them:
If you had listened to me,
you too would not be paying!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the practical difference offered in Step 16.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that under the 'זכאי' wording the minority judge pays his share.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The minority judge disagreed with the mistaken ruling, so he can fairly refuse to pay for it.

steps.title: New difference: do the majority judges cover his share?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא offers a new difference. The minority judge never pays. The question is whether the other judges must pay his share. Under 'זכאי' they do. Under the wording that names each judge, they do not.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the difference is whether the others pay his share. According to the one who writes 'זכאי', they pay it. According to the one who writes 'So-and-so and so-and-so ruled exempt, and so-and-so ruled liable', they don't pay it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא accepts that the minority judge doesn't pay. It moves the difference to whether the majority judges must cover his portion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the verdict just says 'זכאי', it looks like a unanimous ruling. So the majority judges carry the whole payment, including his share. If the verdict names who voted which way, everyone can see that he dissented. Then nobody pays his share.

keyTerms.meaning: There is a difference between them

phrases.english: Rather, the difference between them is
whether they must pay his share:
phrases.notes: 'They' are the two majority judges, and 'his share' belongs to the outvoted judge.

phrases.english: according to the one who says 'exempt' – they pay,
according to the one who says 'So-and-so and so-and-so exempt
and so-and-so and so-and-so obligate' – they do not pay.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא, אִיכָּא בֵּינַיְיהוּ לְשַׁלּוֹמֵי אִינְהוּ מְנָתָא דִּידֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the rejected difference from Step 16 with a new one.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The minority judge pays his own share under 'זכאי'.
steps.terutzMaskana: He never pays. The question is whether the majority judges cover his share.

steps.title: Why should the majority judges pay his share?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא attacks the new difference. The majority judges can tell the minority judge that without him there would have been no verdict at all, so he should share the payment.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to the one who writes 'זכאי', do the others really pay his share? Let them say to him: 'If you hadn't been with us, the case would never have reached a verdict!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer from Step 18.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two judges alone cannot decide a case like this, so the third judge was needed for any verdict to exist. That makes him partly responsible. So the majority judges should not have to cover his share.

keyTerms.meaning: The judgment would have been completed

phrases.english: And according to the one who says 'exempt,' they pay?
Let them say to him:
If you had not been with us,
the judgment would not have been concluded at all!
phrases.notes: Two judges alone couldn't make a verdict, so his presence made the ruling possible.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the difference offered in Step 18.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that under 'זכאי' the majority judges pay the minority judge's share.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The minority judge was needed to complete the court, so he shares the responsibility and the majority need not cover his share.

steps.title: The difference is only wording, because of רכילות
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes that there is no money difference at all. The argument is only about the wording. רבי יוחנן writes just 'זכאי' because of the איסור of 'לא תלך רכיל'.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the difference between them is because of 'You shall not go as a talebearer among your people.' רבי יוחנן says to write 'זכאי' because of 'You shall not go as a talebearer.'
steps.whatsHappening: After both money-based differences were knocked down, the גמרא gives a final answer. The dispute is about avoiding רכילות when writing the verdict.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Naming which judges voted each way would reveal private information and could cause bad feelings. That is רכילות. So רבי יוחנן writes only 'זכאי', and the payment rules stay the same for both opinions.

keyTerms.meaning: Do not go around as a talebearer (ויקרא 19:16)

steps.whatToRemember: The verdict says only 'זכאי' (רבי יוחנן) so the judges don't reveal who voted which way. That would be רכילות. The dispute is about wording, not about who pays.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that even judges are bound by the איסור of רכילות when they write a verdict.

phrases.english: Rather, the difference between them is
because of 'You shall not go as a talebearer among your people.'
phrases.notes: ויקרא 19:16

phrases.english: Rabbi Yoḥanan says: 'Exempt' –
because of 'You shall not go as a talebearer.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא, אִיכָּא בֵּינַיְיהוּ מִשּׁוּם ״לֹא תֵלֵךְ רָכִיל בְּעַמֶּיךָ״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Drops the money-based differences and explains the dispute as being about wording.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Moves the dispute from money to wording and ethics
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The dispute affects who pays for a mistaken ruling.
steps.terutzMaskana: The dispute is only about whether naming the judges counts as רכילות. רבי יוחנן writes just 'זכאי' to avoid it.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רבי יוחנן writes only 'זכאי' so that individual votes are not revealed, because of 'לא תלך רכיל'.

steps.title: ריש לקיש names the judges so the document is not misleading
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש says the verdict should list which judges voted for each side. Writing only 'זכאי' would look like a lie.
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש says they write: 'So-and-so and so-and-so find him not liable, and so-and-so and so-and-so find him liable.' The reason is that writing only 'not liable' would look like a lie.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the answer from the last step. It now gives ריש לקיש's reason for naming every judge's vote.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 20 gave רבי יוחנן's reason: naming judges spreads gossip, so he writes only 'זכאי'. Here we get the other side. A plain 'זכאי' sounds like every judge agreed, which is not true, so ריש לקיש spells out the split. The argument is about honest wording, not about money.

keyTerms.meaning: So-and-so; a stand-in for a real name

phrases.english: Reish Lakish said:
"So-and-so and so-and-so find him not liable,
and so-and-so and so-and-so find him liable" —
because otherwise it looks like a lie.
phrases.notes: Writing just 'not liable' sounds like all the judges agreed, and they didn't.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes step 20's answer by giving the reason for ריש לקיש's side.
steps.terutzResolutionType: The argument is about wording only, and each side has its own reason
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought the two wordings might lead to a money difference
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי יוחנן avoids gossip, and ריש לקיש avoids a misleading document

steps.title: רבי אלעזר combines both concerns in one wording
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר accepts both reasons. So the court writes: 'From their words, so-and-so was found not liable.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר agrees with this master and with that master. So they write: 'From their words, so-and-so was found not liable.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר takes both concerns seriously. He gives a middle wording that solves both problems.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Like רבי יוחנן, he does not name who voted which way, so there is no gossip. Like ריש לקיש, the phrase 'from their words' does not claim that everyone agreed, so it is not a lie.

keyTerms.meaning: He holds of that master's view

steps.whatToRemember: Final wording of a split verdict: 'מדבריהם נזדכה פלוני'. It names no one, and it does not claim the judges all agreed.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Elazar holds of this master,
phrases.notes: He means רבי יוחנן's worry about gossip.

phrases.english: and holds of that master.
phrases.notes: And also ריש לקיש's worry about looking like a lie.

phrases.english: Therefore, they write like this:
"From their words, so-and-so was found not liable."

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר אִית לֵיהּ דְּמָר, וְאִית לֵיהּ דְּמָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the two reasons from steps 20 and 21 and merges them into one wording.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The verdict is written 'מדבריהם נזדכה פלוני', which avoids both gossip and a false impression.

steps.title: Who is brought back in after the judges decide?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה, 'they would bring them in', and asks whom. It cannot mean the litigants, because they were in the room the whole time.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says that when the judges finished, they would bring them in. Whom? If you say the litigants, they are already standing there!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to a new line of the משנה. It asks what 'bring them in' refers to, and rules out the obvious guess.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You can only bring in someone who was sent out. The two sides in the case never left the courtroom, so the משנה cannot be talking about them. This sets up the answer in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: They finished the matter, meaning the judges reached a decision
The two sides in the court case

phrases.english: They finished the matter,
they would bring in, etc.
Whom?
If you say the litigants —
they are standing there!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic by going back to the next line of the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Who is brought back into the courtroom after the judges decide?

steps.title: The witnesses are the ones brought back in
steps.stepSummary: Since the litigants never left, the משנה must mean the witnesses.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it means the witnesses.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its own question: the people brought back in are the witnesses.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The witnesses were sent out of the room earlier, so they are the ones who need to be brought back. This answer leads straight to the next question: which תנא holds this?

phrases.english: Rather, the witnesses.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 23.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The משנה means the witnesses are brought back in.

steps.title: Whose opinion does this fit? Not רבי נתן's
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which תנא the משנה follows. It answers that it does not follow רבי נתן.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whose opinion is this? It is not like רבי נתן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks which opinion fits a משנה that brings the witnesses back in. It says the משנה does not go like רבי נתן, and it is about to bring a ברייתא to show why.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Bringing the witnesses back in for the verdict seems to treat their testimony as one joined unit. There is an argument about how strictly two witnesses must be joined. The גמרא places this משנה on the stricter side, away from רבי נתן.
steps.confusionAlert: רבי נתן's own view has not been quoted yet. The ברייתא starts in the next step, and his opinion comes in step 27.

phrases.english: According to whom?
Not according to Rabbi Natan,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on step 24's answer (the witnesses) to ask which opinion the משנה follows.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which תנא's opinion fits a משנה that brings the witnesses back in?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: It does not fit רבי נתן.

steps.title: The ברייתא about joining two witnesses' testimony
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא says two witnesses' testimony only joins if they saw the event together. רבי יהושע בן קרחה says it joins even if they saw it one after the other.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught in a ברייתא: their testimony never joins together unless both of them saw it at the same time. רבי יהושע בן קרחה says: even if they saw it one after the other.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts quoting the ברייתא that shows the argument behind step 25. This part covers the first two opinions, about seeing the event.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first opinion is strict: two witnesses count as a pair only if they saw the event together. רבי יהושע בן קרחה is more lenient: they may have seen it at different times. The ברייתא keeps going after this point, and רבי נתן's view comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: Joins together into one valid testimony

phrases.english: As it was taught in a baraita:
Their testimony never joins together
unless the two of them saw it together.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha says:
Even one after the other.
phrases.notes: Each witness saw the event at a different moment, and their testimony still joins.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings the source that step 25 relies on when it says the משנה does not follow רבי נתן.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that the משנה does not follow רבי נתן
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא listing opinions about when two witnesses' testimony joins together

steps.title: רבי נתן allows witnesses to testify on different days
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues. The first opinion requires both witnesses to testify together. רבי נתן says one can testify today and the other tomorrow.
steps.simpleTranslation: And their testimony does not stand in court unless both of them testify together as one. רבי נתן says: we hear this one's words today, and when the other comes tomorrow, we hear his words.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes quoting the ברייתא it started in the last step. This part shows that רבי נתן does not require the witnesses to testify together.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If רבי נתן lets witnesses testify on separate days, he would not need them brought back together for the verdict. So a משנה that brings the witnesses in together cannot follow רבי נתן. This completes the proof begun in step 25.

phrases.english: And their testimony does not stand in court
unless the two of them testify together as one.
Rabbi Natan says:
We hear the words of this one today,
and when his fellow witness comes tomorrow,
we hear his words.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֵין עֵדוּתָן מִתְקַיֶּימֶת בְּבֵית דִּין עַד שֶׁיָּעִידוּ שְׁנֵיהֶן כְּאֶחָד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the ברייתא quoted in step 26.
steps.raayaObject: That the משנה (witnesses brought in together for the verdict) does not follow רבי נתן.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא in which רבי נתן allows each witness to testify on a different day.

steps.title: The משנה really means the litigants, following רבי נחמיה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא takes back its reading. The משנה can mean the litigants after all, and it follows רבי נחמיה.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, really it means the litigants, and the משנה follows רבי נחמיה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects what it said in step 24 and goes back to reading 'bring them in' as the litigants. It is setting up a source to show how that can work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 23, the litigants were ruled out because they never left the room. The גמרא now says there is a תנא, רבי נחמיה, who holds that the litigants were sent out. If so, bringing them back in makes sense.

keyTerms.meaning: really, actually (the original reading was right)
the litigants, the two sides in the case

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is reversing itself here. 'לא' means 'No, what we said before is wrong.' The litigants are back in the picture.

phrases.english: No, really it means the litigants.
And it follows Rabbi Nechemya,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects step 24's claim that the משנה must mean the witnesses.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The conclusion that 'bring them in' must mean the witnesses.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: It assumed the litigants were never sent out. According to רבי נחמיה, they were.

steps.title: The custom of the careful people of ירושלים
steps.stepSummary: רבי נחמיה describes the custom. Litigants and witnesses were heard, then everyone was sent out while the judges discussed the case, then they were brought back in.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is taught: רבי נחמיה says, this was the custom of the careful-minded people of Jerusalem. They brought in the litigants and heard their words. They brought in the witnesses and heard their words. They took them outside and discussed the matter. When they finished the matter, they brought them in, and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the ברייתא of רבי נחמיה to back up the new reading. It shows that the litigants were taken out of the room.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since everyone, litigants included, was sent outside during the discussion, the משנה's 'bring them in' can mean bringing the litigants back for the verdict. This solves the problem from step 23.

phrases.english: As it is taught: Rabbi Nechemya says,
This was the custom
of the careful-minded people of Jerusalem:
they bring in the litigants and hear their words,
and they bring in the witnesses and hear their words,
and they take them outside
and discuss the matter.

phrases.aramaic: גָּמְרוּ אֶת הַדָּבָר, מַכְנִיסִין אוֹתָן כּוּ׳.
phrases.english: When they finished the matter, they bring them in, etc.
phrases.notes: 'Them' here means the litigants, who come back in to hear the verdict.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּתַנְיָא: רַבִּי נְחֶמְיָה אוֹמֵר, כָּךְ הָיָה מִנְהָגָן שֶׁל נְקִיֵּי הַדַּעַת שֶׁבִּירוּשָׁלַיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source for step 28's claim.
steps.raayaObject: That the litigants were sent out, so the משנה's 'bring them in' can mean the litigants.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא of רבי נחמיה describing the custom in Jerusalem.

steps.title: A ברייתא says the witnesses are brought in
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the new reading. A ברייתא explicitly says that when they finished, they brought in the witnesses.
steps.simpleTranslation: But it is taught: when they finished the matter, they bring in the witnesses!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a challenge against reading the משנה as the litigants. Another ברייתא clearly says it was the witnesses who were brought in.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a ברייתא openly says 'witnesses', it seems the משנה's 'them' should also mean witnesses. That would bring back the problem that the משנה does not fit רבי נתן.

phrases.english: But it is taught: When they finished the matter,
they bring in the witnesses!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָתַנְיָא: גָּמְרוּ אֶת הַדָּבָר, מַכְנִיסִין אֶת הָעֵדִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reading from steps 28-29.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the court brings the litigants back in for the verdict.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא explicitly says the witnesses are brought back in, not the litigants.

steps.title: That ברייתא does not follow רבי נתן
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא which mentions witnesses indeed does not follow רבי נתן.
steps.simpleTranslation: That ברייתא is not like רבי נתן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. Yes, that ברייתא talks about witnesses, but it simply follows the view that disagrees with רבי נתן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Bringing the witnesses back together only fits the view that requires them to testify together, which is not רבי נתן's view. That ברייתא can stay as it is. Our משנה can still be read as the litigants, following רבי נחמיה.
steps.whatToRemember: There are two ways to read 'bring them in.' If it means the witnesses, it does not follow רבי נתן. If it means the litigants, it follows רבי נחמיה, who says everyone was sent out during the discussion.

phrases.english: That one is not in accordance with Rabbi Natan.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 30.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Assigns the conflicting source to a different תנא.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא about witnesses forces us to read our משנה as the witnesses too.
steps.terutzMaskana: That ברייתא follows the view against רבי נתן, so our משנה can still mean the litigants, following רבי נחמיה.

steps.title: Back to the ברייתא: must the witnesses see the event together?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the ברייתא itself. The first opinion says the testimonies join only if both witnesses saw the event together. רבי יהושע בן קרחה says they join even if they saw it one after the other.
steps.simpleTranslation: The matter itself: their testimony never joins unless the two of them saw the event together. רבי יהושע בן קרחה says: even one after the other.
steps.whatsHappening: Using the word 'גופא', the גמרא goes back to discuss the ברייתא from step 26 on its own terms. It repeats the argument to set up a question about it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before, the ברייתא was used only as a proof about רבי נתן. Now the גמרא wants to understand the argument about seeing the event itself. This is a new discussion, not just a repeat.

keyTerms.meaning: the matter itself (returning to discuss a source directly)

steps.confusionAlert: This argument is about SEEING the event at different times. The earlier argument with רבי נתן was about TESTIFYING in court at different times. They are two separate questions.

phrases.english: The matter itself:
Their testimony never joins together
unless the two of them saw it together.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha says:
Even one after the other.

steps.triggerLanguage: גּוּפָא: לְעוֹלָם אֵין עֵדוּתָן מִצְטָרֶפֶת עַד שֶׁיִּרְאוּ שְׁנֵיהֶם כְּאֶחָד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the discussion of the משנה and returns to the ברייתא from step 26 to discuss it directly.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The תנא קמא requires both witnesses to see the event together. רבי יהושע בן קרחה allows them to see it one after the other.

steps.title: What is the argument about?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the root of the disagreement is.
steps.simpleTranslation: About what do they disagree?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what basic point makes the two תנאים argue.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא wants the reason behind each side, not just the ruling. Knowing the root helps us see why each one holds what he does.

keyTerms.meaning: what is the root of their argument?

phrases.english: About what do they disagree?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reasoning behind the argument quoted in step 32.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The underlying basis of the argument between the תנא קמא and רבי יהושע בן קרחה.

steps.title: Either a פסוק or logic
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the argument can be explained as being about a פסוק, or as being about logic.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you want, say it is about a פסוק. And if you want, say it is about logic.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives two possible roots for the argument, one from a פסוק and one from reasoning. This sets up the next steps, where each option will be explained.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase 'איבעית אימא' means there are two equally good ways to explain it. The details of each way have not been given yet. They come next.

keyTerms.meaning: if you want, say (offers one of two explanations)

phrases.english: If you wish, say it is about a verse,
and if you wish, say it is about logic.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא קְרָא, וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא סְבָרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 33 in outline form and sets up the explanations that follow.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The argument can rest on how a פסוק is read, or on logical reasoning. Each will be explained next.

steps.title: The logic-based reason for the argument
steps.stepSummary: The first opinion holds that each witness speaks about a different hundred, so each event has only one witness. רבי יהושע בן קרחה holds that both witnesses are really testifying that a hundred is owed, so their testimonies join.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you want, say they argue about logic. The first opinion says the hundred this witness talks about is not the hundred the other witness talks about, so each event has only one witness. The other opinion, רבי יהושע בן קרחה, says both of them are simply testifying that a hundred is owed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the first possible root of the argument: plain logic about what each witness is actually saying.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first opinion looks at the specific event each witness saw. Two separate events, each seen by only one witness, do not add up to two witnesses. רבי יהושע בן קרחה looks at the bottom line: both agree the borrower owes a hundred, and that shared claim is enough to join them.

keyTerms.meaning: Logic or reasoning, as opposed to a source from a פסוק
A hundred (dinars), the amount in the case
And the other one, meaning the other opinion

steps.confusionAlert: Don't read 'this one does not testify' as saying either witness is lying. Each one is honest. The question is only whether two witnesses to two different events can count together as a pair.

phrases.english: If you wish, say it is about logic:
About the hundred that this one testifies about,
phrases.notes: Here 'מנה' means a hundred dinars of debt. Each witness saw a different loan of a hundred.

phrases.english: that one does not testify,
and the hundred that that one testifies about,
this one does not testify.
And the other opinion:
phrases.notes: This is רבי יהושע בן קרחה.

phrases.english: both are testifying about a hundred in general.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Fills in the first of the two explanations promised in step 34 (logic).
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The argument is whether witnesses to separate events of a hundred count as one testimony (רבי יהושע בן קרחה: yes, both say a hundred is owed) or as two single witnesses (first opinion).

steps.title: The פסוק-based reason begins
steps.stepSummary: Alternatively, the argument comes from the פסוק 'והוא עד או ראה או ידע' (ויקרא 5:1).
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say they argue about a פסוק, as it is written: 'and he is a witness, whether he saw or knew.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the second possible root of the argument: a פסוק. It is setting up an explanation that it will build in the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק calls the testimony 'עד', a single witness, and then says 'saw or knew'. To use this פסוק, the גמרא first needs to show what the word 'עד' means in the תורה. That is why a ברייתא comes next.

phrases.english: And if you wish, say it is about a verse,
as it is written:
"and he is a witness, whether he saw or knew."
phrases.notes: ויקרא 5:1

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers the second explanation from step 34 (a פסוק) as an alternative to the logic in step 35.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The argument is rooted in how to read 'והוא עד או ראה או ידע'.

steps.title: A ברייתא asks why the תורה says 'one witness'
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא points out that 'לא יקום עד' already sounds like one witness, so it asks why the פסוק adds the word 'אחד'.
steps.simpleTranslation: And it was taught in a ברייתא: from the fact that it says 'a witness shall not rise up', don't I already know it means one? So why does the פסוק say 'one'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to explain the word 'עד'. The ברייתא opens with a question about an extra word in a פסוק, and that question sets up its rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'עד' is singular, so 'אחד' seems unnecessary. The ברייתא treats the extra word as a sign that 'עד' on its own does not automatically mean one witness.

keyTerms.meaning: Why does the פסוק need to say this? (pointing to an extra word)

phrases.english: And it was taught:
From the implication of what is said:
"A witness shall not rise up"
phrases.notes: דברים 19:15. The full פסוק says 'לא יקום עד אחד'.

phrases.english: do I not know that it is one?
What does the verse teach by saying "one"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a ברייתא to explain the word 'עד' in the פסוק quoted in step 36.
steps.raayaObject: The meaning of the word 'עד' in 'והוא עד או ראה או ידע'
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא on 'לא יקום עד אחד' (דברים 19:15)

steps.title: 'עד' in the תורה means two witnesses
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא answers that the extra 'אחד' teaches a general rule: wherever the תורה says 'עד', it means two, unless it says 'אחד'.
steps.simpleTranslation: This set up a general rule: every place the תורה says 'witness', it means two, unless the פסוק specifically tells you 'one'.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers its own question by drawing a general rule from the extra word 'אחד'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because the תורה had to add 'אחד', plain 'עד' must mean a full set of two witnesses. So in 'והוא עד או ראה או ידע', the single word 'עד' refers to two witnesses. That is the base the גמרא needs to connect the פסוק to the argument about witnesses who saw the event one after the other.

keyTerms.meaning: Set up a general rule (a model to apply everywhere)

steps.whatToRemember: There are two ways to explain the argument. By logic: do witnesses to two separate loans of a hundred join because both say a hundred is owed? By a פסוק: the ברייתא teaches that 'עד' in the תורה means two witnesses unless the פסוק says 'אחד'.
steps.whyThisMatters: This rule about 'עד' is used across the תורה. It lets the word 'עד' in 'והוא עד או ראה או ידע' be read as describing two witnesses.

phrases.english: This built a general rule:
Every place where "witness" is said,
there are two here,
unless the verse specifies for you "one".

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the ברייתא's question from step 37.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The extra 'אחד' teaches that a plain 'עד' in the תורה means two witnesses.

steps.title: The singular word teaches that both must see it together
steps.stepSummary: The תנא קמא explains that the תורה uses the singular word עד for two witnesses to teach that they must both see the event as one.
steps.simpleTranslation: The תורה wrote it in singular language to teach that the testimony counts only if both witnesses saw the event together, as one.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes explaining how the תנא קמא gets his view from the פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 38 taught that עד in the תורה means two witnesses. The תנא קמא asks why the תורה calls two witnesses by a singular word. He answers that it teaches the two must act like one: they must see the event at the same moment.

keyTerms.meaning: expressed it, put it in words
the Merciful One, meaning the תורה
the two of them as one

phrases.english: And the Merciful One expressed it in singular language,
phrases.notes: He means the תורה calls two witnesses by the singular word עד.

phrases.english: to say: only when the two of them saw it as one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the rule from Step 38 (עד means two) to show where the תנא קמא gets his view.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The singular form for two witnesses teaches that they must see the event together.

steps.title: The other view: testimony works in any case
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע בן קרחה learns from 'והוא עד או ראה או ידע' that a witness counts however he saw or knew, so the two need not see together.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the other opinion learns from 'And he is a witness, whether he saw or knew' that the testimony counts in any case.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now gives the source for רבי יהושע בן קרחה, who allows witnesses who saw separately to be joined.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'או ראה או ידע' show that a witness counts whether he saw or only knew. So it does not matter if the two witnesses saw at different times. Each one's knowledge counts, and they join.

keyTerms.meaning: in any case, no matter how

phrases.english: And the other opinion,
phrases.notes: This is רבי יהושע בן קרחה.

phrases.english: "And he is a witness, whether he saw or knew" –
phrases.notes: ויקרא 5:1

phrases.english: in any case.

steps.whatToRemember: The תנא קמא says witnesses must see the event together, learned from the singular word עד. רבי יהושע בן קרחה says they need not, learned from 'או ראה או ידע'.
steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִידַּךְ, וְהוּא עֵד אוֹ רָאָה אוֹ יָדָע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the other side's source, finishing the explanation that began in Step 36.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'או ראה או ידע' teaches that testimony is valid in any case, even if the witnesses saw at different times.

steps.title: Must the witnesses testify at the same time?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא brings a new argument: the תנא קמא says both witnesses must testify together, and רבי נתן says one may testify today and the other tomorrow.
steps.simpleTranslation: Their testimony does not stand in court unless both of them testify together as one. רבי נתן says: we hear this one's words today, and when his friend comes tomorrow, we hear his words.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the ברייתא and quotes its next line, which brings a new argument about testifying in בית דין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier argument was about seeing the event. This one is about speaking in בית דין. The תנא קמא needs both witnesses in court together, while רבי נתן lets בית דין hear them on different days and still join them.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two arguments. Before, the question was about SEEING the event together. Now it is about TESTIFYING in בית דין together.

phrases.english: And their testimony does not stand in court
unless the two of them testify as one.
Rabbi Natan says:
We hear the words of this one today,
and when his fellow comes tomorrow
we hear his words.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the argument about seeing together to a new argument in the same ברייתא about testifying together.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: תנא קמא: witnesses must testify together in court. רבי נתן: they may testify on different days and be joined.

steps.title: What is the reason for this argument?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the תנא קמא and רבי נתן are really arguing about.
steps.simpleTranslation: About what do they disagree?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the root of the argument. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא gave the two rulings without reasons. The גמרא wants to know what idea leads each תנא to his view.

phrases.english: About what do they disagree?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reasoning behind the argument quoted in Step 41.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The underlying basis of the argument between the תנא קמא and רבי נתן.

steps.title: Logic or a verse: two ways to explain
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the argument can be explained either as being about logic or as being about a פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you want, say it is about logic; if you want, say it is about a verse.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives two possible roots for the argument. It will now explain each one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the same pattern used in Step 34 for the first argument. The גמרא offers two ways to understand the argument and will spell them out one by one.

phrases.english: If you want, say it is logic,
if you want, say it is a verse.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא סְבָרָא, אִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא קְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 42 in general terms.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The argument may come from logic or from a פסוק.

steps.title: The logic of the first opinion: one witness only brings an oath
steps.stepSummary: The תנא קמא reasons that a single witness who comes alone only makes the defendant swear. He cannot bring a money payment, so his words cannot later be joined to another witness.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you want, say it is logic: One master holds that when one witness comes, he comes for an oath, not for money.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the logic side, starting with the תנא קמא who requires both witnesses to testify together.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When one witness testifies alone, the law is that he can only make the defendant take a שבועה. Two witnesses are needed to make him pay ממון. So the תנא קמא holds that a witness who came alone already counts as a 'שבועה witness' and cannot be joined with a second witness who comes later to make a payment.

phrases.english: If you want, say it is logic:

phrases.aramaic: מָר סָבַר, עֵד אֶחָד כִּי אָתֵי –
phrases.english: One master holds: when one witness comes –
phrases.notes: This is the תנא קמא.

phrases.english: he comes for an oath,
he does not come for money.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא סְבָרָא: מָר סָבַר, עֵד אֶחָד כִּי אָתֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the 'logic' option from Step 43 for the תנא קמא.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A lone witness's testimony only brings a שבועה, so it cannot be joined later to make someone pay.

steps.title: רבי נתן's reply: בית דין joins them anyway
steps.stepSummary: רבי נתן argues that even witnesses who come together speak one at a time, and בית דין joins their words. So בית דין can also join them when they come on different days.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the other says: Is it that when they come together they testify with one mouth? Rather, we join them. Here too, let us join them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives רבי נתן's logic, which pushes back against the reasoning of the תנא קמא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two witnesses never speak with one mouth. Even in the same session, one talks and then the other, and בית דין combines them. If joining works for one after the other on the same day, רבי נתן says it should work for one today and one tomorrow too.

keyTerms.meaning: is that to say? (a question that expects 'no')

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that joining two testimonies is something בית דין does, not something that happens just because the witnesses stand in court together. That is why רבי נתן allows testimony on different days.

phrases.english: And the other:
phrases.notes: This is רבי נתן.

phrases.english: Is that to say that when they come together,
they testify with one mouth?
Rather, we join them.
Here too, let us join them.

steps.whatToRemember: תנא קמא: a lone witness only brings a שבועה, so witnesses must testify together. רבי נתן: witnesses always speak one at a time and בית דין joins them, so different days are fine.
steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִידַּךְ: אַטּוּ כִּי אָתוּ בַּהֲדֵי הֲדָדֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives רבי נתן's logic, which answers the reasoning of the תנא קמא in Step 44.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Since בית דין always joins separate statements, it can join statements given on different days too.
steps.kashyaTarget: The תנא קמא's idea that a lone witness cannot be joined to another.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Even witnesses in the same session speak separately and are joined, so being separate is not a problem.

steps.title: The second explanation: the argument comes from a פסוק
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives its second way of explaining the argument. The תנא קמא and רבי נתן disagree about how to read the פסוק "אם לוא יגיד ונשא עונו".
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you prefer, say that they are arguing about a פסוק: "If he does not tell, he shall carry his sin."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא switches from the logic explanation to the second explanation it promised, which is based on a פסוק. This line only quotes the פסוק. How each side reads it comes on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 43 the גמרא said the argument could be about logic or about a פסוק. Steps 44-45 covered logic. Here the גמרא names the פסוק both sides will use, the one about a witness who must come forward and testify, but it has not yet shown how each side reads it.

keyTerms.meaning: "And if you wish, say": brings in a second, alternate explanation
A פסוק, a verse from the תורה
"If he does not tell": a witness who keeps his testimony to himself
"He shall carry his sin": he is held responsible for staying silent

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new argument. It is the same argument from step 41, now explained in a second way, through a פסוק instead of through logic.

phrases.english: And if you wish, say: they argue about a verse:
phrases.notes: This is the second option from step 43. The first option, logic, was already explained in steps 44-45.

phrases.english: "If he does not tell, then he shall bear his iniquity,"
phrases.notes: ויקרא 5:1

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the logic explanation (steps 44-45) to the second, פסוק-based explanation promised in step 43.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What are the תנא קמא and רבי נתן arguing about (asked in step 42)?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Second answer: they disagree about how to read the פסוק "אם לוא יגיד ונשא עונו". The details follow on the next amud.
